claim: A presigned URL grants time-limited access to an object without changing the bucket policy. The URL uses the credentials of the IAM principal who generated it.
question: What does a presigned URL do, and whose credentials does it carry?

values.display: time-limited access to objects in Amazon S3 without updating your bucket policy
the credentials used by the presigned URL are those of the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) principal who generated the URL
time-limited access

evidence.quote: You can use presigned URLs to grant time-limited access to objects in Amazon S3 without updating your bucket policy. A presigned URL can be entered in a browser or used by a program to download an object. The credentials used by the presigned URL are those of the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) principal who generated the URL.

claim: Anyone with valid security credentials can create a presigned URL, but the URL only works if its creator has permission to perform the operation the URL is for. A presigned URL is limited by the permissions of the user who created it.
question: Who can create a presigned URL, and what permissions does it carry?

values.display: anyone with valid security credentials can create a presigned URL
limited by the permissions of the user who created it
presigned URLs are bearer tokens

evidence.quote: Anyone with valid security credentials can create a presigned URL. But for someone to successfully access an object, the presigned URL must be created by someone who has permission to perform the operation that the presigned URL is based upon.

The capabilities of a presigned URL are limited by the permissions of the user who created it. In essence, presigned URLs are bearer tokens that grant access to those who possess them. As such, we recommend that you protect them appropriately.

claim: A presigned URL made with temporary credentials expires when those credentials expire, even if the URL was given a later expiration time. For an IAM role, the URL expires when the role session expires.
question: Why does a presigned URL made by a Lambda function or EC2 role stop working before its expiration time?

values.display: the URL expires when the credential expires
the presigned URL expires when the role session expires, even if you specify a longer expiration time

qualifiers.scope: presigned URLs made with temporary security credentials
qualifiers.condition: temporary credentials (IAM role, EC2 instance role, STS)

evidence.quote: If you created a presigned URL using a temporary credential, the URL expires when the credential expires. In general, a presigned URL expires when the credential you used to create it is revoked, deleted, or deactivated. This is true even if the URL was created with a later expiration time.
The presigned URL expires when the role session expires, even if you specify a longer expiration time.

claim: A presigned URL can let someone upload a specific object to your bucket without having AWS credentials or permissions of their own. If an object with the same key already exists, S3 replaces it with the uploaded object, and after the upload the bucket owner owns the object.
question: Can a browser upload directly to S3 with a presigned URL, and what does the uploader need?

values.display: without requiring another party to have AWS security credentials or permissions
Amazon S3 replaces the existing object with the uploaded object
the bucket owner will own the object

evidence.quote: You may use presigned URLs to allow someone to upload an object to your Amazon S3 bucket. Using a presigned URL will allow an upload without requiring another party to have AWS security credentials or permissions.

When someone uses the URL to upload an object, Amazon S3 creates the object in the specified bucket. If an object with the same key that is specified in the presigned URL already exists in the bucket, Amazon S3 replaces the existing object with the uploaded object. After upload, the bucket owner will own the object.

claim: A presigned URL can be used many times until its expiration date and time. S3 checks the expiration at the time of the HTTP request, so a download that started before expiry continues past it.
question: Is a presigned URL single-use, and what happens to a download in progress when the URL expires?

values.display: use the presigned URL multiple times, up to the expiration date and time
checks the expiration date and time of a signed URL at the time of the HTTP request

evidence.quote: You can use the presigned URL multiple times, up to the expiration date and time.

Amazon S3 checks the expiration date and time of a signed URL at the time of the HTTP request. For example, if a client begins to download a large file immediately before the expiration time, the download continues even if the expiration time passes during the download.

claim: With a Requester Pays bucket, the requester instead of the bucket owner pays for the request and the data download. The bucket owner always pays for storing the data.
question: With Requester Pays, who pays for requests and downloads, and who still pays for storage?

values.display: the requester instead of the bucket owner pays the cost of the request and the data download
the bucket owner always pays the cost of storing data
Requester Pays

qualifiers.condition: Requester Pays enabled on the bucket

evidence.quote: With Requester Pays buckets, the requester instead of the bucket owner pays the cost of the request and the data download from the bucket. The bucket owner always pays the cost of storing data.

claim: A Requester Pays bucket does not allow anonymous access; every request must be authenticated so that S3 can identify and charge the requester.
question: Can anonymous users read a Requester Pays bucket?

values.display: anonymous access to that bucket is not allowed
you must authenticate all requests involving Requester Pays buckets

evidence.quote: If you enable Requester Pays on a general purpose bucket, anonymous access to that bucket is not allowed.
You must authenticate all requests involving Requester Pays buckets. The request authentication enables Amazon S3 to identify and charge the requester for their use of the Requester Pays bucket.

claim: A requester must include the x-amz-request-payer header (or the RequestPayer parameter) to show they accept the charges. Without it, S3 returns a 403 error and charges the bucket owner for the request.
question: What must a request to a Requester Pays bucket include, and what happens without it?

values.display: x-amz-request-payer
Amazon S3 returns a 403 error and charges the bucket owner for the request

qualifiers.scope: per request to a Requester Pays bucket
qualifiers.condition: bucket owners do not need to add the header

evidence.quote: To show they accept the charges, requesters must either include `x-amz-request-payer` as a header in their API request for DELETE, GET, HEAD, POST, and PUT requests, or add the `RequestPayer` parameter in their REST request.
If `x-amz-request-payer` is not in the request, Amazon S3 returns a 403 error and charges the bucket owner for the request.

claim: Transfer Acceleration is a bucket-level feature for fast transfers over long distances between a client and a general purpose bucket. It uses CloudFront edge locations: data arrives at an edge location and is routed to S3 over an optimized network path.
question: What is S3 Transfer Acceleration, and how does it speed up transfers?

values.display: bucket-level feature that enables fast, easy, and secure transfers of files over long distances
globally distributed edge locations in Amazon CloudFront
routed to Amazon S3 over an optimized network path

evidence.quote: Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration is a bucket-level feature that enables fast, easy, and secure transfers of files over long distances between your client and an S3 general purpose bucket. Transfer Acceleration is designed to optimize transfer speeds from across the world into S3 general purpose buckets. Transfer Acceleration takes advantage of the globally distributed edge locations in Amazon CloudFront. As the data arrives at an edge location, the data is routed to Amazon S3 over an optimized network path.

claim: Use Transfer Acceleration when customers upload to one central bucket from all over the world, when you move gigabytes to terabytes across continents regularly, or when you cannot use all your available bandwidth when uploading to S3.
question: When is Transfer Acceleration the right answer?

values.display: upload to a centralized general purpose bucket from all over the world
transfer gigabytes to terabytes of data on a regular basis across continents
can't use all of your available bandwidth over the internet when uploading

evidence.quote: Your customers upload to a centralized general purpose bucket from all over the world.
You transfer gigabytes to terabytes of data on a regular basis across continents.
You can't use all of your available bandwidth over the internet when uploading to Amazon S3.

claim: Each upload through Transfer Acceleration is checked; if acceleration is not likely to be faster than a regular transfer to the same Region, AWS does not charge for Transfer Acceleration on that transfer and may bypass it.
question: Are you charged for Transfer Acceleration when it would not be faster?

values.display: we will not charge for the use of S3 Transfer Acceleration for that transfer
we may bypass the S3 Transfer Acceleration system for that upload

qualifiers.condition: when acceleration is not likely to be faster than a regular transfer

evidence.quote: If we determine that S3 Transfer Acceleration is not likely to be faster than a regular Amazon S3 transfer of the same object to the same destination AWS Region, we will not charge for the use of S3 Transfer Acceleration for that transfer, and we may bypass the S3 Transfer Acceleration system for that upload.

claim: To use Transfer Acceleration you must send requests to the bucket-name.s3-accelerate.amazonaws.com endpoint; the regular endpoints keep standard transfer. The bucket name must be DNS-compliant and must not contain periods.
question: What endpoint and bucket name rules does Transfer Acceleration require?

values.display: s3-accelerate.amazonaws.com
must not contain periods

evidence.quote: The name of the bucket used for Transfer Acceleration must be DNS-compliant and must not contain periods (".").

To access the bucket that is enabled for Transfer Acceleration, you must use the endpoint `{{bucket-name}}.s3-accelerate.amazonaws.com`. Or, use the dual-stack endpoint `{{bucket-name}}.s3-accelerate.dualstack.amazonaws.com` to connect to the enabled bucket over IPv6. You can continue to use the regular endpoints for standard data transfer.

claim: Transfer Acceleration is the better choice when higher throughput is wanted. For objects smaller than 1 GB or a data set under 1 GB, AWS says to consider CloudFront PUT/POST instead.
question: When should you choose CloudFront PUT/POST over Transfer Acceleration?

values.display: a better choice if a higher throughput is desired
smaller than 1 GB

qualifiers.condition: object or data set size under 1 GB

evidence.quote: S3 Transfer Acceleration optimizes the TCP protocol and adds additional intelligence between the client and the S3 bucket, making S3 Transfer Acceleration a better choice if a higher throughput is desired. If you have objects that are smaller than 1 GB or if the data set is less than 1 GB in size, you should consider using Amazon CloudFront's PUT/POST commands for optimal performance.

claim: Multipart upload uploads one object as a set of parts that can be sent independently and in any order; a failed part is retransmitted without affecting the others, and S3 assembles the object when all parts are uploaded. AWS calls it a best practice for objects of 100 MB or larger.
question: How does multipart upload improve throughput and resilience, and from what size is it recommended?

values.display: upload a single object to Amazon S3 as a set of parts
retransmit that part without affecting other parts
100 MB or larger

evidence.quote: Multipart upload allows you to upload a single object to Amazon S3 as a set of parts. Each part is a contiguous portion of the object's data. You can upload these object parts independently, and in any order.

If transmission of any part fails, you can retransmit that part without affecting other parts. After all parts of your object are uploaded, Amazon S3 assembles them to create the object. It's a best practice to use multipart upload for objects that are 100 MB or larger instead of uploading them in a single operation.

claim: A started multipart upload has no expiry; you must explicitly complete or stop it. Until you do, you are billed for storage of the uploaded parts.
question: What happens to the parts of a multipart upload that is never completed?

values.display: there is no expiry; you must explicitly complete or stop the multipart upload
stop incurring charges for storage of the uploaded parts

evidence.quote: After you initiate a multipart upload, there is no expiry; you must explicitly complete or stop the multipart upload.

After you initiate a multipart upload and upload one or more parts, you must either complete or stop the multipart upload to stop incurring charges for storage of the uploaded parts. Only *after* you complete or stop a multipart upload will Amazon S3 free up the parts storage and stop billing you for the parts storage.

claim: A lifecycle rule with the AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload action stops multipart uploads that are not completed within a set number of days after they started, and deletes their parts. AWS recommends this rule as a best practice to minimize storage costs; it applies to existing and future multipart uploads and never deletes objects.
question: How do you clean up incomplete multipart uploads automatically, and why?

values.display: AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload
stops the multipart upload and deletes the parts
no objects are deleted by this lifecycle action

qualifiers.condition: the number of days after initiation is set in the rule

evidence.quote: As a best practice, we recommend that you configure a lifecycle rule by using the `AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload` action to minimize your storage costs.

When a multipart upload isn't completed within the specified time frame, it becomes eligible for an abort operation. Amazon S3 then stops the multipart upload and deletes the parts associated with the multipart upload. This rule applies to both existing multipart uploads and those that you create later.

Also, this action doesn't apply to objects. No objects are deleted by this lifecycle action. Additionally, you will not incur early delete charges for S3 Lifecycle when you remove any incomplete multipart upload parts.

claim: S3 Batch Operations runs one operation on a list of objects you specify; a single job can act on billions of objects, and S3 tracks progress, sends notifications and stores a completion report.
question: What is S3 Batch Operations?

values.display: perform a single operation on lists of Amazon S3 objects that you specify
a single job can perform a specified operation on billions of objects
tracks progress, sends notifications, and stores a detailed completion report

evidence.quote: S3 Batch Operations can perform a single operation on lists of Amazon S3 objects that you specify. A single job can perform a specified operation on billions of objects containing exabytes of data. Amazon S3 tracks progress, sends notifications, and stores a detailed completion report of all actions, providing a fully managed, auditable, and serverless experience.

claim: Batch Operations can copy objects, update their server-side encryption, set object tags or ACLs, start restores from S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, and invoke a Lambda function for custom actions. The object list comes from a custom list or an S3 Inventory report.
question: Which operations can an S3 Batch Operations job run?

values.display: copy objects, update server-side encryption of objects, and set object tags or access control lists (ACLs)
initiate object restores from S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or invoke an AWS Lambda function
use an Amazon S3 Inventory report to easily generate lists of objects

evidence.quote: Use S3 Batch Operations to copy objects, update server-side encryption of objects, and set object tags or access control lists (ACLs). You can also initiate object restores from S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or invoke an AWS Lambda function to perform custom actions using your objects. You can perform these operations on a custom list of objects, or you can use an Amazon S3 Inventory report to easily generate lists of objects.

claim: A Batch Operations job needs a manifest: an S3 object listing the bucket name, object key and optionally the version of each object, in the form of an S3 Inventory report or a CSV file. S3 can also generate the manifest from object filter criteria you set.
question: What is the manifest of a Batch Operations job?

values.display: an Amazon S3 object that contains the object keys that you want Amazon S3 to act upon
an Amazon S3 Inventory report or a CSV file
you must supply a manifest

evidence.quote: A manifest is an Amazon S3 object that contains the object keys that you want Amazon S3 to act upon. If you want to create a Batch Operations job, you must supply a manifest. Your user-generated manifest must contain the bucket name, object key, and optionally, the object version for each object. If you supply a user-generated manifest, it must be in the form of an Amazon S3 Inventory report or a CSV file.
You can also have Amazon S3 generate a manifest automatically based on object filter criteria that you specify when you create your job.

claim: Directory buckets organize data hierarchically into directories, unlike the flat structure of general purpose buckets; they have no prefix limits and individual directories scale horizontally.
question: How does a directory bucket organize data differently from a general purpose bucket?

values.display: organize data hierarchically into directories
there aren't prefix limits for directory buckets

evidence.quote: Directory buckets organize data hierarchically into directories as opposed to the flat storage structure of general purpose buckets. There aren't prefix limits for directory buckets, and individual directories can scale horizontally.

claim: Directory buckets do not support, among others, S3 Versioning, S3 Replication, S3 Object Lock, MFA delete, Requester Pays, S3 Event Notifications, Lifecycle transition actions, object tags, server access logs, static website hosting and Transfer Acceleration.
question: Which common S3 features are not available on directory buckets?

values.display: not supported by directory buckets
S3 Versioning
S3 Replication
S3 Object Lock

evidence.quote: The following Amazon S3 features are not supported by directory buckets:
Multi-factor authentication (MFA) delete
S3 Lifecycle transition actions

note: The unsupported-feature list is a bullet list on the page; the quote is its lead sentence. Writers should link only the items named in the claim.

claim: S3 Standard, Intelligent-Tiering, Standard-IA, Glacier Instant Retrieval, Glacier Flexible Retrieval and Glacier Deep Archive store objects redundantly on multiple devices across at least three Availability Zones in a Region; S3 One Zone-IA stores data redundantly within a single Availability Zone.
question: How many Availability Zones does S3 use for its storage classes, and which class uses only one?

values.display: a minimum of three Availability Zones in an AWS Region
multiple devices within a single Availability Zone
designed to sustain data in the event of the loss of an entire Amazon S3 Availability Zone

evidence.quote: S3 Standard, S3 Intelligent-Tiering, S3 Standard-IA, S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, and S3 Glacier Deep Archive redundantly store objects on multiple devices across a minimum of three Availability Zones in an AWS Region.
The S3 One Zone-IA storage class stores data redundantly across multiple devices within a single Availability Zone.

S3 Standard, S3 Intelligent-Tiering, S3 Standard-IA, S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, and S3 Glacier Deep Archive are all designed to sustain data in the event of the loss of an entire Amazon S3 Availability Zone.

claim: Versioning preserves, retrieves and restores every version of every object so you can recover from unintended user actions and application failures; by default a request returns the most recently written version. Object Lock and S3 Replication are the other data protection features named beside versioning.
question: Which S3 features protect data, and which version does a plain GET return?

values.display: preserve, retrieve, and restore every version of every object
by default, requests retrieve the most recently written version
Amazon S3 Object Lock and S3 Replication

evidence.quote: You can use versioning to preserve, retrieve, and restore every version of every object that is stored in your Amazon S3 bucket. With versioning, you can easily recover from both unintended user actions and application failures. By default, requests retrieve the most recently written version.
Apart from S3 Versioning, you can also use Amazon S3 Object Lock and S3 Replication to protect your data.

claim: Server access logging gives detailed records of the requests made to a bucket, for security and access audits. CloudTrail data events record object-level API activity such as GetObject, DeleteObject and PutObject for individual buckets.
question: What is the difference between S3 server access logs and CloudTrail data events?

values.display: detailed records of the requests that are made to a bucket
data events record object-level API activity for individual buckets
GetObject, DeleteObject, and PutObject

evidence.quote: Server access logging provides detailed records of the requests that are made to a bucket. Server access logs can assist you in security and access audits, help you learn about your customer base, and understand your Amazon S3 bill.

Data events are records of resource operations performed on or within a resource. In Amazon S3, data events record object-level API activity for individual buckets. CloudTrail supports a subset of Amazon S3 object-level API operations, such as `GetObject`, `DeleteObject`, and `PutObject`.

claim: In a versioned bucket, deleting the current version without a version ID does not permanently delete the object; S3 adds a delete marker, which becomes the current version with a new version ID.
question: What happens when you delete an object in a versioning-enabled bucket without giving a version ID?

values.display: S3 adds a delete marker, issuing a soft delete of the object
Amazon S3 doesn't permanently delete the object
the delete marker then becomes the current (or newest) version of the object

qualifiers.condition: the delete request names no version ID

evidence.quote: For versioned buckets, if you delete the current version of an object or when a delete request doesn’t specify a specific version Id, Amazon S3 doesn’t permanently delete the object. Instead, S3 adds a delete marker, issuing a soft delete of the object. The delete marker then becomes the current (or newest) version of the object with a new version ID.

claim: In an unversioned bucket you delete by key only; in a versioning-enabled bucket you can give the version ID to delete one specific version of the object.
question: How do you delete one specific version of an object?

values.display: provide the version ID of the object to delete a specific version of the object
you provide only the object key name

evidence.quote: When deleting objects from a bucket that is not versioning-enabled, you provide only the object key name. However, when deleting objects from a versioning-enabled bucket, you can provide the version ID of the object to delete a specific version of the object.
